content: Swallowing, scientifically referred to as deglutition, is a reflex mechanism in the human body that facilitates the passage of substances from the mouth to the pharynx and subsequently into the esophagus. This process involves the closure of the epiglottis to prevent entry into the trachea. If this mechanism fails and the object enters the trachea, it can result in choking or pulmonary aspiration. The swallowing process is coordinated by the swallowing center located in the medulla oblongata and pons. The reflex is triggered by touch receptors in the pharynx when a bolus of food is pushed to the back of the mouth by the tongue. Swallowing is a complex mechanism that involves both skeletal muscles, such as the tongue, and smooth muscles of the pharynx and esophagus. The autonomic nervous system (ANS) plays a critical role in coordinating the pharyngeal and esophageal phases of swallowing. Normal swallowing is divided into four distinct phases: the oral preparatory phase, the oral (or buccal) phase, the pharyngeal phase, and the esophageal phase. Not all sources consider the oral preparatory phase as a separate phase. Oral Preparatory Phase: During this phase, food is processed through mastication and combined with tongue movements to form a bolus of appropriate size and consistency for passage through the pharynx and esophagus. Oral (or Buccal) Phase: Once the bolus is ready, it is moved to the back of the tongue. The anterior portion of the tongue elevates against the hard palate and retracts posteriorly to propel the bolus into the oropharynx. The posterior tongue is then elevated by the mylohyoid muscles, which also elevate the soft palate to seal the nasopharynx, preventing nasal aspiration. This phase is voluntary and involves cranial nerves V (trigeminal), VII (facial), and XII (hypoglossal). Pharyngeal Phase: In this phase, the bolus is transported from the pharynx to the esophagus via peristalsis. The soft palate is elevated against the posterior nasopharyngeal wall by the levator veli palatini muscle. The palatopharyngeal folds on either side of the pharynx are brought closer together by the superior constrictor muscles, allowing only a small bolus to pass. The larynx and hyoid are elevated and pulled forward toward the epiglottis, relaxing the cricopharyngeus muscle. This action passively closes the entrance to the larynx, and the vocal cords are drawn together to narrow the airway. This phase is reflexively controlled and involves cranial nerves V, X (vagus), XI (accessory), and XII. During this phase, the respiratory center in the medulla is temporarily inhibited by the swallowing center, a phenomenon known as deglutition apnea. Esophageal Phase: The upper esophageal sphincter relaxes to allow the bolus to pass. Sequential contractions of the striated constrictor muscles of the pharynx, along with peristalsis and relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, propel the bolus through the esophagus into the stomach. In terminally ill patients, failure of the swallowing reflex can lead to the accumulation of mucus or saliva in the throat and airways, producing a sound known as the death rattle or agonal respiration. Clinical Significance: Swallowing becomes a significant concern in elderly individuals, as conditions such as strokes and Alzheimer’s disease can impair the autonomic nervous system's function. Speech therapy is often employed to address these issues, as the neuromuscular structures involved in speech are also utilized in swallowing. Disorders affecting the oral or pharyngeal phases can result in oropharyngeal dysphagia, while disorders of the esophageal phase can lead to esophageal dysphagia.
